claim: All 21 Dprs are predicted to contain two immunoglobulin (IG) domains.
source: All 21 Dprs and nine DIPs are predicted to contain two and three immunoglobulin (IG) domains, respectively (Figure 1a).
evidence: Based on prediction from sequence analysis and shown in Figure 1a

claim: All nine DIPs are predicted to contain three immunoglobulin (IG) domains.

claim: Most Dprs contain signal sequences at their N termini.
source: Despite the lack of conservation, most Dprs and DIPs contain signal sequences at their N termini, and hydrophobic patches, likely to be transmembrane helices or GPI linkage sites, at or close to their C termini.
evidence: Stated based on sequence analysis of Dpr proteins

claim: Most DIPs contain signal sequences at their N termini.

claim: Most Dprs contain hydrophobic patches, likely to be transmembrane helices or GPI linkage sites, at or close to their C termini.

claim: Most DIPs contain hydrophobic patches, likely to be transmembrane helices or GPI linkage sites, at or close to their C termini.

claim: Dprs and DIPs are predicted to be cell surface glycoproteins.
source: Therefore, we predict Dprs and DIPs to be cell surface glycoproteins.

claim: The first IG domains (IG1) mediate the Dpr–DIP interaction.
source: Our previous work identified the first IG domains, termed IG1, as the domains mediating the Dpr–DIP interaction by the formation of a pseudo-symmetric IG1-IG1 heterocomplex using the GFCC'C' face of the immunoglobulin fold (Carrillo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by previous work cited as Carrillo et al., 2015

claim: Dpr–DIP interaction is mediated by the formation of a pseudo-symmetric IG1-IG1 heterocomplex using the GFCC'C' face of the immunoglobulin fold.

claim: Closely related Dprs interact with the same DIPs.
source: Dpr and DIP sequences covering the IG domains can be aligned within each of the families to create phylogenetic trees, which demonstrate that closely related Dprs interact with the same DIPs, and closely related DIPs interact with the same set of Dprs (Özkan et al., 2013) and Figure 1b)

claim: Closely related DIPs interact with the same set of Dprs.

evidence: Based on crystal structure analysis from cited work

claim: The average root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of all IG1 Cα atoms within the three complex structures (Dpr1–DIP-η, Dpr6–DIP-α, Dpr11–DIP-γ) is 0.78 Å (±0.14).

claim: The pairwise sequence identities among the three Dpr–DIP pairs (Dpr1–DIP-η, Dpr6–DIP-α, Dpr11–DIP-γ) are comparable, ranging from 49% to 56%.

claim: Different Dpr–DIP complexes can be established through small but significant movements of the Dpr and DIP monomers with respect to each other.

claim: Heterophilic binding allows for higher diversity in neuronal recognition than homophilic binding.
